title: "Modelling Match State and Player Performance in the Big Bash League"
format: pdf
editor: visual

### Abstract

Historical ball-by-ball data from the Big Bash League (BBL) was used to examine how match situations affect scoring, wickets and player performance. The analysis combines data exploration and statistical modelling to study different stages and situations within T20 matches. An interactive dashboard was developed to explore scoring rates, wicket patterns and batter performance across teams, opponents, seasons and different match situations. Logistic regression was also used to estimate the probability of winning during run chases. These probabilities were then used to group match situations into pressure levels and compare batter performance under different levels of pressure.


The project also examines whether the likelihood of a wicket can be predicted before a delivery and which bowlers perform best during the death overs after accounting for the situations in which they bowl. An XGBoost model was used to predict the probability of a wicket on each delivery using match-state, recent performance and player-related features. Mixed-effects models were used to compare death-over bowlers based on their ability to restrict runs and take wickets, while accounting for differences in match state, batters and venues. Together, these analyses provide a better understanding of how player performance changes across different match situations and demonstrate how data exploration and statistical modelling can be used to analyse BBL performance.

### Introduction

T20 cricket is a fast-paced format in which match situations can change quickly and individual deliveries can have a significant impact on the result. Each team has a maximum of 20 overs to score runs which means the batting team must balance scoring quickly with preserving wickets. Playing too cautiously can leave too many runs to score later in the innings, while being too aggressive can result in losing wickets and reducing the team's ability to accelerate. As a result, player performance is better understood when it is considered together with the match situation in which it occurs

This is particularly important during a run chase. The batting team must consider how many runs are still required, how many deliveries remain and how many wickets are available. Together, these factors influence the difficulty of the chase and the decisions made by batters. Similarly, bowling performance can also depend on the stage and state of the innings, since restricting runs or taking wickets may be more difficult under some match situations than others.

Traditional statistics such as batting averages, strike rates and bowling economy rates provide useful measures of player performance. However, these measures do not fully account for the match context in which the performance occurred. Combining traditional performance measures with ball-by-ball match-state information can therefore provide a more detailed understanding of how players and teams perform under different conditions.

This project examines match state and player performance in the Big Bash League (BBL) using historical ball-by-ball data. The delivery-level structure of the data allows matches to be analysed as they develop, rather than only through final match or innings summaries.

### The overall project consisted of six key research questions which were divided among the three members of the group. 
1. How do scoring rates and wicket probabilities vary across the three phases of a T20 innings — the Powerplay (overs 1–6), the middle overs (7–16), and the death overs (17–20)?

2. Can we build a model that predicts the probability of a wicket falling on any given delivery, using match-state and player-identity features?

3. Which batters perform best under high-pressure chase situations — defined by a high required run rate and few wickets in hand — relative to their performance in low-pressure situations?

4. Which bowlers are most effective at restricting runs and taking wickets in the death overs, after controlling for the match state they bowl in?

5. Does winning the toss and choosing to field (the more common decision in T20) actually translate into a meaningful advantage?

6. Do players naturally cluster into distinct batting or bowling archetypes based on their ball-by-ball performance profiles?

#### ### Data provided

Data for the project was obtained from CricSheet, which provided ball-by-ball data. For the analysis, two datasets were provided through bbl_all.csv and bbl_match_info.csv.

The main dataset bbl_all.csv contained the ball-by-ball information for BBL matches, with **each observation representing one delivery**. It included information such as the match, season, innings, batting and bowling teams, striker, non-striker, bowler, runs scored from the bat, extras, wides, no-balls, byes, leg-byes, wickets, type of dismissal and venue. This dataset gave a very detailed record of what happened on each delivery. However, many of the variables needed to answer my research questions were not directly available. For example, the data did not directly provide the current match score, run rate, number of wickets remaining, balls remaining, required run rate, match phase or a measure of pressure. These variables therefore had to be created through feature engineering.

The second dataset bbl_match_info.csv contained information at the match level with each observation representing one match. This included variables such as the target runs and the winner of the match. These variables were important particularly for the second research question, as the target was required to calculate the required run rate and the match winner was required to create the binary win/loss outcome for the pressure model.

The two datasets were therefore used together. The ball-by-ball dataset provided the changing match state after every delivery, while the match-level dataset provided the final match information needed to understand the result of the chase. In the feature-engineering stage, the target information was joined to the delivery-level dataset using the match ID.

### Analysis

1.1 BBL format vs traditional format

Before getting into the deeper analysis, lets understand how a T20 innings is usually structured and why the different parts of the innings matter. Traditionally, a T20 innings is looked at in three phases they are Powerplay from overs 1–6, Mid-Game from overs 7–16 and Death Overs from overs 17–20. This traditional phase structure was followed throughout the analysis so that the same method could be used across all seasons in the dataset.

Each phase usually has a different style of play. During the Powerplay, only a limited number of fielders are allowed outside the inner circle which generally gives the batting team more opportunities to attack and score boundaries. The bowling team has fewer options to protect the boundary during this period so the first few overs can often be more favourable to the batting side. Once the Powerplay ends the fielding team gets more freedom to spread the field and helps them restrict the batting team from getting scoring more which changes how both teams approach the game.

The Mid-Game usually becomes more about controlling the innings. Batters may focus more on rotating strike, building partnerships and avoiding unnecessary wickets while bowlers try to reduce the scoring rate and build pressure. In the Death Overs the situation changes again because only a few overs remain. Batting teams generally become much more aggressive and try to maximise the final score while bowling teams focus more on limiting boundaries and taking wickets.

However BBL introduced a different Powerplay rule from the 2020–21 season. Under the traditional format, all six Powerplay overs were played at the beginning of the innings. After the BBL rule change, only the first four overs remained as the opening Powerplay. The remaining two overs became the Power Surge, which could be taken by the batting team from the 11th over onwards. During the Power Surge, the same fielding restriction applied, with only two fielders allowed outside the inner circle.

This made the BBL more complicated to analyse across different seasons because the fielding restrictions were no longer attached to the same overs throughout the entire dataset. Before the rule change overs 1–6 represented the full Powerplay. After the rule change only overs 1–4 followed the Powerplay restrictions, while the other two restricted overs could appear later in the innings depending on when the batting team chose to use the Power Surge. Because the exact Power Surge period was not available in the data used the traditional 1–6, 7–16 and 17–20 phase structure was continued so that the historical comparison remained consistent across all seasons.

2.1 Feature Engineering - Dashboard

Before answering both research questions a major part of the work was feature engineering. The raw ball-by-ball data gave detailed information about what happened on every delivery but by itself it did not completely describe the situation of the match at that point. For example the data contained runs scored from the bat, extras, wickets and player information but important match-state variables such as the current score, current run rate, wickets already lost, number of legal balls completed and the phase of the innings were not directly available. Since both research questions depend heavily on understanding what was happening in the match at a particular point these variables first had to be derived from the available information.

The main idea was to convert the raw delivery data into something that followed the actual flow of an innings. The deliveries were first arranged in the correct order within every match and innings. From the delivery information, the over number was identified and each delivery was assigned to the traditional match phase of Powerplay, Mid-Game or Death Overs. The target from the match-level dataset was also joined using the match ID so that deliveries in the second innings could be connected with the score that the batting team was trying to chase.

Once the deliveries were in the correct order the match situation could be reconstructed. Runs scored from the bat and extras were combined to calculate the total runs from each delivery. A separate wicket indicator was also used to show whether a wicket had been lost on that ball where retired hurt not treated as a dismissal. From these two variables, cumulative runs and cumulative wickets could then be calculated after every delivery and combined into the normal cricket score format such as 85/3. This was important because instead of only knowing what happened on one delivery, the data could now show how the actual scoreboard was changing throughout the innings.

The same idea was also applied to extras and match phases. Cumulative values were calculated for wides, no-balls, byes and leg-byes while runs and wickets were also tracked separately within Powerplay, Mid-Game and Death Overs. This became particularly useful for the first research question because the aim was not only to look at the final result of an innings but also to understand how scoring and wickets changed as the match moved from one phase to another.

Another important part was correctly identifying legal deliveries. A row in the dataset does not always represent a legal ball because wides and no-balls can add runs to the score without counting as one of the six legal deliveries in an over. Because of this simply counting rows would give an incorrect number of balls bowled. A legal-delivery indicator was therefore used to separate legal balls from wides and no-balls and the cumulative number of legal deliveries was calculated throughout the innings. This later became important for calculating run rate and also for the second research question where balls remaining and required run rate depend on the number of legal deliveries that have actually been completed.

The match situation before each delivery was also important. For this reason runs before the current ball and wickets before the current ball were derived from the cumulative values. This was mainly required for the pressure analysis because the pressure faced by a batter should represent the situation before the delivery is bowled. For example, if a batter hits a six on a delivery, that six should not already be included when calculating the pressure they were facing before that ball. Using the state before the delivery helped make sure that the analysis represented the information that was actually available at that point in the match.

Using cumulative runs and cumulative legal deliveries, the current team run rate could then be calculated after each ball. This gave a continuously changing measure of how quickly the batting team was scoring instead of only calculating one run rate at the end of the innings.

One of the most important parts throughout this entire feature-engineering process was grouping the data correctly. Almost every cumulative calculation or summary had to be calculated within the correct match and innings. At the most basic level, variables such as cumulative runs and wickets were grouped by match_id and innings so that the calculations restarted when a new innings or match began. If this grouping was not done correctly the score from one innings could continue into another and the entire match state would become incorrect. For later analysis, additional variables such as season, batting team, bowling team, over and match phase were added depending on what was being calculated.

Overall, the feature engineering was mainly about converting individual delivery records into a proper representation of the match. The raw data showed what happened on each ball while the derived variables showed where the match stood at that point. Once the score, wickets, legal balls, run rate, phases and before-ball match state were available the data could then be used properly for the scoring-rate, wicket and pressure analyses that followed.

The direction taken to answer these research questions was through an interactive dashboard. Instead of focusing on predicting what might happen in a future BBL match, the dashboard analysis focused more on understanding what has already happened across the historical data available. The idea was to use previous matches to capture scoring, wicket and player-performance patterns and allow the user to explore how these patterns changed depending on the season, team, opposition and match situation. The dashboard therefore acts more as a historical analysis tool rather than a future prediction tool helping users understand how teams and players have performed in different situations over the years.

2.2 Phase Overview -> Score

Before jumping into the deeper scoring rate, wicket and pressure analysis, a clear way to understand how an actual match progressed was first created. For this the scoring progression of both innings was recreated using an interactive line graph in the dashboard. Instead of only looking at the final score the graph shows how both teams moved through the innings over the 20 overs and where the match started shifting in favour of one team and is done so by using a simple line graph

The user can select a season and then choose a particular match from that season. Both innings are then plotted together which makes it easier to compare how the two teams were scoring at each phase of the innings. Wickets are also shown on the graph and the Powerplay, Mid-Game and Death Overs are separated in the background. The graph is interactive so when the user hovers over different points they can see more information about what was happening at that stage of the match.

The main purpose of this graph was to give a simple overall picture of the match before moving into the more detailed analysis. It helps the user first understand how the score developed, where wickets were lost and how the match moved through different phases before looking at deeper historical patterns in scoring rates, wickets and pressure situations.

2.3 How do scoring rates and wicket patterns vary across the different phases of a T20 innings?

2.3A Phase Overview -> Scoring Rate -> Run Rate Progression Tab

Before going into the wicket analysis the aim was first to understand how a team has historically scored against a particular opponent across the innings. For that the Scoring Rate section was created in the dashboard and one of the main tabs inside it is the Run Rate Progression tab.

In this tab the user selects a base team and an opponent. The graph then shows how the cumulative run rate of the base team changes over the course of the innings against that selected opponent. If a specific season is selected, the graph only uses the matches played in that season. If the season filter shows "---" it means the analysis is across all seasons, so all matches between those two teams in the dataset are taken together which has around data from season of 2011/12-2024/25.

The line in the graph represents the cumulative run rate progression across the innings. At each over cumulative run rate is calculated as the total runs scored up to that point/over divided by the total number of legal balls faced up to that point/over and then multiplied by 6. This was used because it gives a clearer picture of how the overall scoring rate develops from the Powerplay to the Mid-Game and Death Overs rather than looking only at individual overs. When a particular season is selected the graph gives a more specific view of the matches played between the selected teams in that season and is very insightful given the two teams have played more than once or twice and while selecting "---" combines all available seasons to show the broader historical scoring pattern between the two teams.

The way the line moves is also important. If the line goes up, it means the team is scoring at a faster rate as the innings progresses. If it becomes flat, it means the scoring rate is staying more stable. If it slightly drops, it means the team had a slower period and the cumulative run rate reduced compared to earlier overs. This makes it easy to understand how the innings develops across the Powerplay, Mid-Game and Death Overs.

The coloured background also helps interpret the innings visually. The blue section represents the Powerplay, the grey section represents the Mid-Game, and the pink section represents the Death Overs. This makes it easier to see in which phase the scoring rate increases, slows down or remains stable.

The three boxes shown below the graph give a summary of the same information by phase. The Powerplay Run Rate box gives the run rate for overs 1 to 6, the Mid-Game Run Rate box gives the run rate for overs 7 to 16 and the Death Run Rate box gives the run rate for overs 17 to 20. So while the graph shows the scoring pattern continuously across the innings these boxes summarise the scoring rate within each phase. These boxes mainly help when filtered match wise more than cumulative so it helps understand in each match what each team is able to get the run rate against the opponent in each phase of the match.

2.3B Phase Overview -> Scoring Rate -> Over Run Rate Progression 

The next tab inside the Scoring Rate section is the Over Run Rate tab. While the previous graph showed the cumulative run rate progression across the innings this tab focuses on each over separately. This was added because sometimes the cumulative graph can smooth out what is happening whereas this graph helps clearly identify which exact overs a team has historically scored faster or slower against a particular opponent.

Here again, the user selects a base team, an opponent and optionally a season. If a particular season is selected the graph only uses the matches from that season. If the season filter shows "---" that means it is using the all-seasons view so all the matches between the selected teams in the dataset are combined together.

The line in this graph represents the run rate for each over individually from over 1 to over 20. In other words, this is not cumulative. For each over, the total runs scored in that over across the selected matches were calculated, divided by the total number of legal balls bowled in that over, and multiplied by 6. So each point on the graph shows how quickly the team has historically scored in that specific over against that specific opponent.

Because this graph is over-by-over, the movement of the line is interpreted a bit differently from the previous tab. If the line rises at a certain over, it means that over has historically produced a higher scoring rate. If it falls, it means scoring was relatively slower in that over. This makes it easier to pick out overs where the batting team tends to accelerate, slow down, or face more difficulty.
This is useful because in T20 cricket, not all overs are played in the same way. Some overs may be more attacking, some may be more controlled, and some may be more wicket-prone. So instead of just saying a team scored well in the Powerplay or Death Overs overall, this graph goes one step deeper and identifies the exact overs where the scoring pattern changes.

The summary boxes below the graph give an even simpler interpretation of the same results. The Highest Run Rate Over box shows the over in which the selected team historically scored at the fastest rate, along with the run rate and total runs scored in that over. The Lowest Run Rate Over box shows the slowest scoring over. The Most Wicket-Prone Over box identifies the over in which the team lost the most wickets, while the Least Wicket-Prone Over box shows the over where the fewest wickets fell.

Overall, this tab helps understand over-level scoring behaviour rather than innings-level progression. It gives a much more detailed historical view of how a team has performed against a particular opponent and helps identify the overs where scoring is strongest, weakest, or where wickets tend to fall more often.

2.3C Phase Overview -> Wicket Analysis -> By over & By Wickets

The next part of the dashboard focuses on wicket analysis which is divided into two views: By Over and By Bowler. The same filters are used here as in the scoring-rate analysis. The user can select a season, a base team and an opponent. If a particular season is selected, only matches from that season are included. If the season filter shows "---", the analysis combines all the available matches between the selected teams across all seasons.

The By Over tab shows how many wickets the selected batting team has historically lost in each over against the chosen opponent. Each bar represents one over from 1 to 20, while the height of the bar represents the total number of wickets lost in that over across the selected matches. The background is again separated into Powerplay, Mid-Game and Death Overs so that the wicket pattern can be connected back to the different stages of the innings. This makes it easier to identify overs where wickets have historically fallen more often and whether those wickets are concentrated in a particular phase of the game.

For example a higher bar in the Death Overs does not automatically mean that the over itself causes more wickets. Teams are usually trying to score much more aggressively towards the end of an innings, which can naturally increase the chance of losing wickets. Because of this, the graph is mainly used to capture historical wicket patterns rather than predict the probability of a wicket falling in a future match.
The By Bowler tab takes the same idea one step further and looks at the bowlers who have historically taken wickets against the selected batting team. Instead of grouping the wickets by over, the wickets are grouped by bowler and the bowlers are arranged based on the number of wickets they have taken against that opponent. Only wickets that can be credited to the bowler are included, so dismissals such as run outs are not counted as a bowler's wicket.

One important thing to keep in mind while using the all-seasons option is that BBL squads are not fixed across seasons. Players can move between teams, leave the competition or join a team in a later season. Because of this, when "---" is selected, the bowler graph represents the historical players who have taken wickets for that team across the full period available in the dataset. This means that a player may still appear in the graph even if they are not part of the current squad because they represented that team and took wickets against the selected opponent in an earlier season.

This was also one of the reasons both the season-specific and all-season options were kept. The season filter allows the user to understand the bowlers and wicket patterns relevant to a particular season, while the all-season option gives a broader historical picture of the matchup between the two franchises. Together, the By Over and By Bowler views help explain not only when wickets have historically fallen, but also which bowlers were responsible for those wickets.


3.1	Which batters perform better under high-pressure chase situations compared with low-pressure situations?

The second research question was a bit more complicated because pressure was not directly available in the dataset. Unlike runs, wickets or overs there was no variable which directly showed whether the batter was playing under high pressure or low pressure. So before comparing the batters, a way to measure how difficult the match situation was at every point of the chase first had to be found.

This analysis only focuses on the second innings, because this is when the batting team is chasing a target and the match situation can be measured based on how many runs are still required. Shortened or interrupted matches were also removed because the normal 120-ball structure would not correctly represent those matches. 

To understand the situation before every delivery, three main variables were used - required run rate, wickets in hand and balls remaining. Required run rate shows how quickly the team needs to score from that point, wickets in hand shows how many wickets the batting team still has available and balls remaining shows how much time is left in the innings. Using all three variables together gives a much better picture of the match situation than using only one variable.For example - needing 40 runs with 50 balls remaining and eight wickets in hand is very different from needing 40 runs from 20 balls with only three wickets in hand. The number of runs required is the same in both cases, but the difficulty of the chase is completely different. This was the main reason why required run rate alone was not enough to represent pressure. 

After creating these match-state variables a logistic regression model was used to estimate the probability of the chasing team winning from that situation. Logistic regression was used because the final outcome had only two possibilities either the chasing team won or lost. The final result was therefore converted into a binary variable where 1 represented a win and 0 represented a loss. The model then used required run rate, wickets in hand and balls remaining to calculate the probability of winning before each delivery.

Before using the final model the matches were split into training and testing data. Around 80% of the matches were used for training and the remaining 20% were used for testing. One important thing here was that the split used the match ID rather than randomly splitting individual deliveries. This was done so that deliveries from the same match would not be present in both the training and testing data. After training the model the performance was checked using the predicted win probabilities, accuracy, confusion matrix and ROC-AUC. The model values are as follows -

Accuracy – 80.32%, logistic regression achieved a test classification accuracy of 80.32% using 0.5 prob of threshold meaning if predictied probability was higher than 0.5, then that observation would be classified as a win and vice-versa.
Confusion Matrix - 
            Predicted
                 0        1
Actual    0     5103    1901
          1     871     6215

The model correctly classified 5103 losing observations and 6215 winning observations while 1901 losing observations were classified as wins and 871 winning observations were classified as losses.
ROC-AUC Values - The ROC-AUC score was 0.8915 meaning the model was able to separate winning and losing chase situations quite well across different probability thresholds. 

The above was the models performance on the test data, the logistic regression was fit again using the complete pressure data-set. The below is the summary of the model values -
Accuracy – 81.30%, logistic regression achieved in-sample classification accuracy of 81.30%

Confusion Matrix - 
             Predicted
                 0          1
Actual    0     26917    7200
          1     6079     30828
          
Once the final model was created, the predicted win probability from each delivery was converted into a pressure score using 1 - predicted win probability. This means a situation with a high chance of winning would have a lower pressure score, while a situation with a low chance of winning would have a higher pressure score. The pressure scores were then divided using the 25th and 75th percentiles, where the bottom 25% was classified as Low Pressure, the top 25% as High Pressure and the middle 50% as Medium Pressure. These pressure levels were then used to compare how each batter performed under different chase situations.


3.2 Batsmen Pressure Analysis

Once the pressure level was calculated for every delivery the next step was to use that and compare how each batter performed under low-pressure and high-pressure chase situations. The final result of this analysis is shown in the Batsmen Pressure Analysis tab of the dashboard.

The dashboard has two filters, Team A and Team B, where the user can select any two teams which have played against each other. Once the teams are selected, the graph shows the batters from both teams who have experienced both low-pressure and high-pressure situations while chasing against that opponent.
The graph compares the batter's strike rate under the two pressure levels across all the available seasons. The grey bar represents low pressure and the green bar represents high pressure. So if the green bar is longer than the grey bar, it means that batter historically scored at a higher rate when the match situation was classified as high pressure. If the grey bar is longer, it means the batter scored faster in lower-pressure situations.

The main comparison here is not really between one player and another, but between the two bars of the same player. A player may not have the highest strike rate overall, but if their high-pressure strike rate is much higher than their low-pressure strike rate, it shows that their scoring rate increased when the match situation became more difficult.

The analysis was kept across all seasons because once the data was split into batter, opponent and pressure level, the number of observations became much smaller. If the analysis had also been split season by season, some batters would have had very few balls under either high or low pressure, which would make the comparison less useful.

One thing to keep in mind here as well is that the players shown here do not represent one fixed squad throughout all seasons. BBL squads change regularly and players can move between teams. So this graph represents the historical performance of batters in that team matchup, not the current squad of either team.

The graph is also interactive. When the user hovers over the bars, it shows more information such as runs scored, balls faced and number of chase matches included in that pressure level. For the high-pressure situations, it also shows the average required run rate, average wickets in hand, average balls remaining and average target. This was added because strike rate alone does not tell the full story. These extra values help the user understand what kind of match situations the batter was actually facing.

Overall, the purpose of this graph is not to simply say that one player is a good or bad pressure player. It is mainly used to understand how the same batter has historically performed when the chase became easier or more difficult based on the pressure score created from the model.


### Findings

The dashboard was mainly used to answer the research questions by allowing the user to explore the historical data under different situations. Because the results change depending on the team, opponent, season and match situation selected there is not one single finding that can be applied to the complete BBL dataset. For example the scoring rate or wicket pattern seen for one team against a particular opponent may be completely different for another matchup. Because of this, the purpose of the analysis was not to conclude that one particular phase always has the highest scoring rate or that wickets always fall more often in one specific over. Instead, the dashboard allows these patterns to be identified depending on the situation the user wants to analyse. The same applies to the batter pressure analysis, where the comparison depends on the batter and opponent selected rather than producing one overall result for every player.

### Limitations of the dashboard, Data and the Analysis

One of the main limitations of the analysis is the difference between the traditional T20 format and the current BBL format. For the complete analysis Powerplay was used as overs 1–6, Mid-Game as overs 7–16 and Death Overs as overs 17–20. However after the Power Surge was introduced in the BBL, only the first four overs remained as the opening Powerplay while the other two overs could be taken later in the innings. Since the exact Power Surge overs were not available in the data the traditional format was used consistently across all seasons. Because of this the phases in the later seasons may not completely represent the actual match conditions.

Another limitation is the limited amount of information available in the dataset. Some important variables which could affect the analysis were either not available or not used, such as the exact Power Surge overs, pitch conditions, weather, batting position, bowling style and player form. Because of this, the analysis mainly focuses on the match-state variables that were available in the ball-by-ball data.

Another thing to keep in mind is that players are not permanent to one BBL team. Players can move between teams, leave the competition or join a team in later seasons. This is especially important when using the all-seasons view because a player shown under a particular team may have represented that team only during certain seasons and may not be part of the current squad.

### Scope for improvement/Future Analysis

The same idea of using the dashboard to understand historical patterns rather than predict future matches could still be maintained, but with more variables the analysis could have gone much deeper. For example, if the exact Power Surge overs were available it would be possible to analyse when each team usually takes the Power Surge against different opponents and what the match situation looks like at that point, such as the score, wickets lost and required scoring rate. This could help understand whether teams have a particular pattern or situation in which they normally decide to use it.

The same analysis could be improved further if information about the type of bowler was available, such as pace, swing or spin. This could help understand whether a team usually takes the Power Surge against a particular type of bowler and how their scoring rate or wickets change during those situations. So instead of changing the overall idea of the dashboard, having more detailed variables would allow the same historical analysis to explain the patterns much better.

Another improvement would be to make the win-probability model more detailed. Right now the model only uses required run rate, wickets in hand and balls remaining. These are important variables but they do not fully explain the difficulty of every chase situation. The model could be improved by adding variables such as the current batter, bowler, partnership, venue, current scoring rate, recent boundaries or wickets and even the target size. This would help the probability estimate represent the actual match situation more closely instead of depending only on three variables. The same pressure analysis could then be built using this improved probability and the comparison between high-pressure and low-pressure batting situations would become much stronger.

Another major improvement would be to combine the match data with weather data before and during the match. Weather can have a large impact on the playing conditions and could help explain some of the scoring and wicket patterns seen in the dashboard. For example, rain or a wet outfield can slow the ball after it is hit, while moisture around the pitch can also change how the ball behaves compared with a dry and sunny day.

If historical weather information was available for each venue and match, variables such as rainfall, temperature and humidity could be combined with the ball-by-ball data. This would allow the dashboard to compare how teams and players have historically performed under different weather conditions and whether scoring rates or wicket patterns change depending on those conditions. This could add another important layer to understanding why the same venue or team matchup may behave very differently from one match to another.
